title: The Merry Adventures of Robin Hood
author: Howard Pyle
openingChapterLabel: How Robin Hood Came to Be an Outlaw
openingText: In Merry England in the time of old, when good King Henry the Second ruled the land, there lived within the green glades of Sherwood Forest, near Nottingham Town, a famous outlaw whose name was Robin Hood. No archer ever lived that could speed a gray goose shaft with such skill and cunning as his, nor were there ever such yeomen as the sevenscore merry men that roamed with him through the greenwood shades.
about:
Howard Pyle (1853–1911) gathered the old ballads of Robin Hood into a single connected story, first published in 1883. Robin becomes an outlaw, wins Little John, Will Scarlet and Friar Tuck to his band, outwits the Sheriff of Nottingham, helps a sorrowful knight, and finally meets King Richard in Sherwood Forest.

Pyle wrote in a deliberately old-fashioned English, with “thee” and “thou” in dialogue and many songs and verses. The chapters read as separate adventures but follow one thread from Robin’s first fight to his epilogue. The preface addresses the reader directly.

whyItMatters.title: A hero who steals from the powerful
whyItMatters.body: Robin takes from the rich bishop and sheriff and gives to the poor. The stories ask what makes an outlaw honorable. Readers can compare the law of Nottingham with the justice of the greenwood, a question every new adaptation answers differently.

whyItMatters.title: Games and tricks drive the plot
whyItMatters.body: Archery contests, disguises, a butcher’s stall and a beggar’s rags move Robin through the stories. The humor comes from watching clever people trick proud ones. Many of the same devices appear in modern heist stories.

whyItMatters.title: A world of songs and old words
whyItMatters.body: Pyle fills the book with ballads, oaths and sharp bargains. The language is partly invented to sound like the Middle Ages. Reading him shows how a nineteenth-century author built a medieval world out of words.

angleCards.title: Follow the disguises
angleCards.text: Note each time Robin or Little John hides who they are and how the trick is exposed or succeeds.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading The Merry Adventures of Robin Hood to follow how disguise drives the plots.

angleCards.title: Weigh the justice
angleCards.text: Ask in each adventure who is wronged, who profits and whether Robin’s side is fair.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading The Merry Adventures of Robin Hood to examine what the stories treat as just and unjust.

angleCards.title: Meet the band
angleCards.text: Compare Little John, Will Scarlet, Friar Tuck and Allan a Dale by how they join Robin.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading The Merry Adventures of Robin Hood to get to know each member of the band.

angleCards.title: Listen to the songs
angleCards.text: Read the verses aloud and notice how they sum up or comment on the action.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading The Merry Adventures of Robin Hood to see what the songs add to the stories.
